title: Bidirectional BFS in London: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS launches two BFS searches—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. On a real street-style grid, it dramatically reduces explored nodes and speeds up pathfinding.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half—watch two searches collide ⚡ Can you feel the speedup? 🚀

Here’s the mechanic (what you’d code):
1) Pick start S and target T.
2) Run BFS forward from S and backward from T at the same time.
3) Always expand the smaller frontier (fewer nodes enqueued).
4) The moment the two visited sets touch, you’ve found the shortest path.

Why it’s faster:
- Plain BFS explores outward in “rings” from S.
- Bidirectional BFS shrinks the rings from both ends, turning the search depth from ~d into ~d/2 on each side.
- In many graphs, that means exploring roughly O(b^(d/2)) instead of O(b^d).

Takeaway: If shortest paths are guaranteed (unweighted graphs), meeting in the middle is one of the cleanest graph optimization moves for interviews.

Debate question: In your experience, when does bidirectional BFS *not* win—tiny graphs, costly visited/set operations, or directed edges?
